questions.stem: Why does a hormone affect only particular target cells?

options.text: Only target cells contain receptors with binding sites for that hormone
options.why: Receptor specificity determines which cells detect the hormone. Cells without the matching receptor don’t begin the pathway.

options.text: Only target cells are supplied with blood carrying that hormone
options.why: Blood can carry a hormone past many cell types. Exposure doesn’t make a cell a target; the matching receptor does.

options.text: Target cells convert every arriving hormone into a receptor protein
options.why: The receptor is already a protein made by the target cell. The ligand binds to it rather than becoming it.

options.text: Target cells admit hormones through any channel in their membrane
options.why: Channels are selective transport proteins, not general entrances for hormones. Many hormones remain outside the cell while signalling.

questions.stem: What causes Vibrio fischeri to produce bioluminescence at high population density?

options.text: The autoinducer reaches a threshold concentration and changes gene expression
options.why: A dense population produces enough autoinducer for receptor activation. The resulting change in gene expression produces the proteins needed for light.

options.text: Individual bacteria detect physical contact and begin aerobic respiration
options.why: Quorum sensing depends on a diffusible chemical’s concentration, not cells touching. Aerobic respiration isn’t the density-detection mechanism.

options.text: The bacteria exhaust the autoinducer and release stored light energy
options.why: The signal accumulates rather than becoming exhausted. Light production follows receptor activation and gene expression.

options.text: A falling nutrient concentration directly opens light-producing ion channels
options.why: The named mechanism uses an accumulating autoinducer and a threshold response. It isn’t caused by opening ion channels.

questions.stem: Which description correctly distinguishes a neurotransmitter from a hormone?

options.text: A neurotransmitter diffuses across a synaptic gap, while a hormone is transported in blood
options.why: This distinguishes their usual routes and distances. Both still act by binding to receptors on target cells.

options.text: A neurotransmitter is always a protein, while a hormone is always a steroid
options.why: Both groups are chemically diverse. Neurotransmitters include amino acids, peptides and amines, while hormones include amines, proteins and steroids.

options.text: A neurotransmitter enters every target cell, while a hormone remains outside
options.why: Membrane crossing depends on chemical properties, not whether the signal is called a hormone or neurotransmitter. Many neurotransmitters stay outside.

options.text: A neurotransmitter acts throughout the body, while a hormone acts only locally
options.why: That reverses the usual contrast. Neurotransmitters act across narrow synaptic gaps, while blood can carry hormones to distant targets.

questions.stem: Which ligand is most likely to bind to an intracellular receptor?

options.text: A hydrophobic steroid that can diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer
options.why: A lipid-soluble steroid can cross the membrane and reach a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

options.text: A large hydrophilic protein that remains dissolved in extracellular fluid
options.why: A hydrophilic protein can’t cross the non-polar center of the bilayer. It normally binds to a transmembrane receptor.

options.text: Acetylcholine released into a synaptic gap beside an ion channel
options.why: Acetylcholine binds to a transmembrane ligand-gated ion channel. It doesn’t cross the postsynaptic membrane to find a receptor.

options.text: Insulin carried in blood to a receptor with tyrosine kinase activity
options.why: Insulin is a protein hormone and binds to a transmembrane insulin receptor. Its signal is relayed by phosphorylation inside the cell.

questions.stem: What directly happens when acetylcholine binds to its postsynaptic receptor?

options.text: An ion channel in the receptor opens, allowing positive ions to enter
options.why: The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel. Positive-ion entry changes the voltage across the postsynaptic membrane.

options.text: The receptor makes cAMP, which carries acetylcholine into the cytoplasm
options.why: That mixes the acetylcholine pathway with GPCR signalling. Acetylcholine opens the receptor channel and stays outside the cell.

options.text: Tyrosine phosphorylation moves glucose transporter vesicles toward the membrane
options.why: That describes insulin receptor signalling. The acetylcholine receptor changes ion permeability instead.

options.text: The receptor enters the nucleus and binds to a specific DNA sequence
options.why: That describes an activated intracellular steroid receptor. An acetylcholine receptor remains in the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.stem: What is the role of a G protein after a ligand activates a GPCR?

options.text: It relays receptor activation to an effector protein on the cytoplasmic side
options.why: The activated G protein interacts with another membrane-associated protein, such as adenylyl cyclase, to continue the pathway.

options.text: It transports the extracellular ligand through the phospholipid bilayer
options.why: The ligand usually remains outside. The G protein transfers information from the activated receptor rather than transporting the ligand.

options.text: It binds directly to DNA and promotes transcription of steroid-response genes
options.why: An activated intracellular receptor can bind specific DNA sequences. A G protein instead relays signals near the plasma membrane.

options.text: It forms a channel that allows positive ions to enter the postsynaptic cell
options.why: That describes a ligand-gated ion channel such as the acetylcholine receptor. G proteins regulate other proteins inside the cell.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes epinephrine signalling through cAMP?

options.text: GPCR activation, G protein activation, adenylyl cyclase activation, cAMP production
options.why: The receptor activates the G protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase. That enzyme converts ATP to the second messenger cAMP.

options.text: Epinephrine entry, intracellular receptor activation, DNA binding, cAMP transcription
options.why: That combines steroid signalling with an impossible final step. Epinephrine stays outside, and cAMP is made from ATP rather than transcribed.

options.text: Ion channel opening, calcium entry, tyrosine phosphorylation, glucose uptake
options.why: These events belong to other signalling routes. The specified epinephrine pathway uses a GPCR, G protein, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP.

options.text: Insulin receptor activation, transporter fusion, ATP release, cAMP breakdown
options.why: That begins with insulin signalling and doesn’t describe epinephrine. cAMP production follows adenylyl cyclase activation.

questions.stem: Why is cAMP called a second messenger in epinephrine signalling?

options.text: It is produced inside the cell after the extracellular ligand activates its receptor
options.why: Epinephrine is the first messenger outside the cell. cAMP relays that signal to intracellular proteins.

options.text: It is the second hormone released by the adrenal gland during exercise
options.why: cAMP isn’t a hormone released into blood. It’s produced and used inside the target cell.

options.text: It carries epinephrine through blood before delivering it to target cells
options.why: Epinephrine travels through blood without cAMP carrying it. cAMP appears only after receptor activation.

options.text: It binds first to the receptor and then passes the receptor to epinephrine
options.why: Epinephrine binds the receptor first. cAMP is produced later on the intracellular side of the pathway.

questions.stem: What is the immediate consequence of activating an insulin receptor?

options.text: Tyrosine residues on the intracellular receptor region become phosphorylated
options.why: The insulin receptor has tyrosine kinase activity. Its phosphorylation starts the intracellular reaction sequence.

options.text: The receptor opens a channel through which glucose and insulin enter
options.why: The insulin receptor isn’t a glucose channel. Its signalling pathway moves separate glucose transporters into the membrane.

options.text: Insulin binds directly to DNA and promotes glucose transporter transcription
options.why: Insulin is a protein hormone that remains outside the cell. Direct DNA binding describes activated intracellular steroid receptors.

options.text: A G protein activates adenylyl cyclase to make the second messenger cAMP
options.why: That describes the specified epinephrine GPCR pathway. Insulin uses a receptor with tyrosine kinase activity.

questions.stem: How does insulin signalling increase glucose entry into a target cell?

options.text: It causes vesicles containing glucose transporters to fuse with the plasma membrane
options.why: Fusion adds more glucose transporters to the membrane. Glucose then enters through them by facilitated diffusion.

options.text: It allows insulin molecules to bind glucose and carry it across the bilayer
options.why: Insulin is a signal rather than a glucose carrier. Membrane transport proteins provide the route for glucose.

options.text: It converts glucose into a hydrophobic molecule that diffuses through phospholipids
options.why: Glucose remains polar and can’t diffuse freely through the bilayer. Transporter proteins are needed.

options.text: It opens the insulin receptor as a glucose-selective ligand-gated channel
options.why: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase, not a glucose channel. Separate transporters move to the membrane.

questions.stem: What does an activated steroid hormone-receptor complex do?

options.text: It binds to specific DNA sequences and regulates gene transcription
options.why: The activated intracellular receptor acts as a regulator of transcription, changing which proteins the target cell produces.

options.text: It opens an ion channel and changes the postsynaptic membrane potential
options.why: That describes acetylcholine binding to a ligand-gated ion channel. Steroid receptors regulate gene expression.

options.text: It activates adenylyl cyclase and converts extracellular ATP into cAMP
options.why: That resembles GPCR signalling, although ATP and cAMP remain intracellular. Steroid-receptor complexes act at DNA.

options.text: It phosphorylates tyrosine and inserts glucose transporters into the membrane
options.why: That describes the insulin receptor pathway. Steroids bind intracellular receptors and regulate transcription.

questions.stem: Which change is an example of positive feedback?

options.text: Oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, which stimulate further oxytocin release
options.why: The response reinforces the initiating stimulus, so the cycle becomes stronger until birth ends it.

options.text: Insulin lowers blood glucose, reducing the stimulus for further insulin secretion
options.why: That’s negative feedback because the response reduces the original high-glucose stimulus.

options.text: A neurotransmitter is removed from a synapse after activating its receptor
options.why: Signal removal limits a response, but this statement doesn’t describe a response reinforcing its own stimulus.

options.text: A G protein hydrolyzes GTP and returns to its inactive state
options.why: GTP hydrolysis switches off G-protein activity. It doesn’t amplify the original stimulus through a feedback loop.
